newsitem.title: TAIWAN: AT&T, Taiwan Far Eastern sign phone deal.
newsitem.headline: AT&T, Taiwan Far Eastern sign phone deal.

text.p: U.S.-based AT&T stepped up its pitch to enter Taiwan's lucrative mobile telephone market on Friday by offering its cross-border "roaming" services to local partner Far Eastern Group.

Under the deal, customers with mobile phones from AT&T-Far Eastern joint venture Far EasTone Telecommunications could use them in 50 countries and regions -- including the United States, Australia and most of Europe.

"It is critical for business people of Taiwan to have the ability to use their phones when they travel abroad, and we're the largest operator in the world," Scott Hooper, president of AT&T Wireless Services, told Reuters in an interview.
But AT&T has to crack the Taiwan market first.

Far EasTone, a T$10 billion (US$363.6 million) venture, is one of 17 groups bidding for eight operation franchises in Taiwan's liberalising mobile telephone market. Far EasTone is seeking two licences -- a northern regional one and a coveted island-wide franchise.
To sweeten its bid, Far EasTone said it would invest eight percent of sales revenue from its Taiwan mobile operation towards local research and development in telecommunication technology.

"We will establish in Taiwan a research and development laboratory that will be second to none in Asia," said Far Eastern Group chairman Douglas Hsu. "While evaluating the bids the government should look at which applicants are the ones showing a commitment to local development."
AT&T's Hooper predicted mobile phone subscribers in Taiwan would skyrocket in 10 years to 10 million from 900,000 now -- accompanied by a significant drop in prices.
"That's what liberalisation is all about: give the consumers more access at a cheaper rate," Hooper said.

Mobile telephony is one of several telecom sectors liberalised by parliament in January, opening them up to private and limited foreign investment. Foreign investors can own stakes of up to 20 percent in Taiwan telecom ventures.

Other telecommunication sectors liberalised in January were paging systems, trunking radio and mobile data, but mobile telephony is by far the most attractive. By comparison, the other sectors have attracted only scant private interest.
"If we get one of the licences, Taiwanese customers would have access to this worldwide system, and we believe this makes us a very strong applicant for the mobile phone market," Hooper said.
Winning bids will be selected before 1997, with new services to rival those offered by state giant Chunghwa Telecom coming on line during 1997.

One major shortcoming under the AT&T plan for Taiwan customers, however, is lack of the ability to "roam" into China -- a crucial market for Taiwan but one where AT&T has yet to sign a cross-border roaming agreement.
Although mobile phones are in wide use on both sides of the Taiwan strait, Taiwan's ban on direct communications between the bitter rivals still prevents cross-strait roaming.

For now, Taiwan and its 21 million people are Far EasTone's priority. The lucrative market, with expected sales of T$18.7 billion or more over the next 10 years, has attracted most of the world's mobile telephone leaders.
Competing with AT&T are U.S. rivals Sprint and Southwestern Bell, Singapore Telecom and Japan's Mitsubishi as well as Taiwan computer giant Acer and the Koo's Group conglomerate.
Far Eastern is one of Taiwan's largest business groups, with 86 subsidiaries, including six that are listed on the Taiwan Stock Exchange.
